questions.stem: What is the architectural difference between one-stage and two-stage detectors?
choices: One-stage uses CNNs, two-stage uses transformers
Two-stage first proposes candidate regions then classifies and refines them; one-stage predicts boxes and classes directly from feature maps in a single pass
One-stage handles only one class
Two-stage requires two GPUs
questions.explanation: Two-stage detectors such as Faster R-CNN generate region proposals and then run a second head on each. One-stage detectors such as YOLO and RetinaNet skip the proposal step and predict everything densely in one pass. The trade has historically been accuracy against speed, though the gap has narrowed considerably.

questions.stem: What is an anchor box?
choices: The ground-truth box
A predefined box of set scale and aspect ratio placed at each feature-map location, which the network refines rather than predicting coordinates from nothing
The largest box in the image
A box drawn by the annotator
questions.explanation: Anchors turn box regression into a correction problem: predict an offset from a sensible prior instead of absolute coordinates. Their scales and ratios encode expectations about object shape, which is why anchor configuration matters and why mismatched anchors hurt recall.

questions.stem: Your dataset consists of very elongated objects such as pipes, and recall is poor with default anchors. What is the fix?
choices: Increase the confidence threshold
Re-cluster anchor scales and aspect ratios on your own training boxes, or use an anchor-free detector
Train for more epochs
Switch to grayscale
questions.explanation: Default anchors are tuned for COCO's shape distribution. If your objects are far more elongated, no anchor overlaps them well enough to be assigned as positive during training, so they are never learned. Clustering anchors on your data, or removing the prior entirely with an anchor-free head, addresses the cause.

questions.stem: What does Intersection over Union measure?
choices: The ratio of correct to incorrect predictions
The overlap between two boxes: their intersection area divided by their union area
The confidence of a detection
The number of objects in an image
questions.explanation: IoU is a scale-invariant overlap measure between 0 and 1. It is used in three distinct places — assigning anchors to ground truth during training, suppressing duplicates in NMS, and deciding whether a detection counts as correct during evaluation — which is why the same threshold value means different things in different contexts.

questions.stem: What does non-maximum suppression do in a detector's post-processing?
choices: Removes low-confidence classes
Keeps the highest-scoring box in each cluster of overlapping detections and discards others above an IoU threshold, removing duplicates of the same object
Thins edges to one pixel
Balances the class distribution
questions.explanation: Dense detectors fire many times around each object. NMS sorts by confidence and greedily suppresses remaining boxes overlapping the winner beyond a threshold. Setting that threshold too low deletes genuinely adjacent objects; too high leaves duplicates.

questions.stem: In a dense crowd, overlapping people are being deleted by NMS. What addresses this without simply raising the IoU threshold everywhere?
choices: Lower the confidence threshold
Soft-NMS, which decays the scores of overlapping boxes instead of removing them outright, so a strongly-supported neighbour survives
Reduce the input resolution
Disable anchors
questions.explanation: Hard NMS makes a binary decision on overlap alone, so genuinely distinct but overlapping objects are lost. Soft-NMS reduces a neighbour's score in proportion to its overlap, letting a confident detection of a second person survive while true duplicates fall below threshold.

questions.stem: What does mean Average Precision summarise?
choices: The mean confidence of all detections
The area under the precision-recall curve for each class, averaged over classes — and in COCO, also averaged over IoU thresholds
The proportion of images with at least one correct detection
The mean IoU of all predictions
questions.explanation: AP integrates precision over recall for one class, capturing the whole operating curve rather than one threshold. mAP averages that across classes. COCO additionally averages over IoU thresholds from 0.5 to 0.95, which is why COCO mAP numbers look much lower than Pascal VOC's single 0.5 threshold.

questions.stem: Which TWO facts about mAP are important when comparing published numbers?
choices: COCO mAP averages over IoU 0.5:0.95, so it is systematically lower than VOC mAP at IoU 0.5
mAP is computed over the whole dataset at all confidence thresholds, so it does not tell you performance at the single threshold you will deploy at
mAP accounts for inference latency
A higher mAP always means better performance on your data
questions.explanation: Comparing a COCO number against a VOC number is comparing different measures. And mAP summarises an entire curve, whereas deployment picks one operating point — a model with higher mAP can be worse at the precision you actually need. Neither latency nor your domain is reflected in the figure.

questions.stem: How does the YOLO family frame detection?
choices: As a two-stage proposal and refinement problem
As a single regression from image to a grid of box coordinates, objectness and class scores, predicted in one forward pass
As pixel-wise classification
As a sequence generation problem
questions.explanation: YOLO divides the image into a grid and predicts boxes, objectness and classes for every cell simultaneously. Seeing the whole image in one pass gives global context and high speed, which is why the family dominates real-time applications.

questions.stem: What is the objectness score in a YOLO-style detector?
choices: The class probability
A per-box estimate of whether any object is present, separate from which class it is
The IoU with the ground truth
The confidence threshold
questions.explanation: Separating presence from identity lets the network suppress the overwhelming majority of background boxes cheaply before class scores matter. Final confidence typically multiplies objectness by class probability, which is why a box can have a strong class score yet low final confidence.

questions.stem: Small objects are missed while large ones are detected well. Which change is most likely to help?
choices: Increase the confidence threshold
Increase input resolution and ensure detection heads operate on high-resolution feature levels — small objects vanish after repeated downsampling
Reduce the number of anchors
Train for fewer epochs
questions.explanation: A 16-pixel object occupies a fraction of a pixel after 32x downsampling, leaving nothing to detect. Higher input resolution preserves it, and a feature pyramid ensures a shallow, fine-grained level is responsible for small scales. Tiling large images at inference is the other standard remedy.

questions.stem: What does a feature pyramid network contribute to detection?
choices: It compresses the model
It combines semantically strong deep features with spatially precise shallow ones via a top-down pathway, so every scale has both context and resolution
It removes the need for anchors
It replaces NMS
questions.explanation: Shallow maps localise well but lack semantics; deep maps know what things are but not precisely where. FPN's top-down path with lateral connections pushes semantics back down, giving each pyramid level both properties. It is one of the highest-impact ideas in modern detection.

questions.stem: How do anchor-free detectors such as FCOS or CenterNet predict boxes?
choices: By enumerating every possible box
By predicting, per location, the distances to the object's boundaries or a centre heatmap plus size, removing anchor hyperparameters entirely
By using a fixed grid of boxes
By segmenting first then fitting boxes
questions.explanation: Rather than refining preset priors, anchor-free heads regress geometry directly from each position — four boundary distances in FCOS, a centre peak plus width and height in CenterNet. This removes anchor scale, ratio and matching-threshold tuning, one of the fiddliest parts of anchor-based training.

questions.stem: Why is IoU loss often preferred to L1 loss on box coordinates?
choices: It trains faster
L1 treats each coordinate independently and its magnitude depends on object size, whereas IoU loss directly optimises the overlap that evaluation measures and is scale-invariant
IoU loss has no gradient issues
L1 cannot be computed on boxes
questions.explanation: Coordinate regression optimises a proxy: the same pixel error is trivial on a large box and severe on a small one, and four independent errors can combine into a poor overlap. IoU-family losses align training with the metric. Variants like GIoU and DIoU add gradient signal when boxes do not overlap at all.

questions.stem: Which TWO choices control the precision-recall trade-off at inference without retraining?
choices: The confidence threshold on detections
The NMS IoU threshold
The learning rate
The augmentation policy
questions.explanation: Both are post-processing knobs. Raising confidence increases precision and loses recall. The NMS threshold governs how aggressively overlapping boxes are merged, trading duplicates against missed neighbours. Learning rate and augmentation only affect training.

questions.stem: A safety system must not miss defects, and a human reviews every alert. How should the operating point be set?
choices: Maximise mAP
Set a low confidence threshold to maximise recall, accepting more false positives because review capacity absorbs them and a missed defect is the costly error
Set a high threshold for precision
Use the default threshold
questions.explanation: The operating point follows the asymmetry of costs, not the benchmark. When a miss is expensive and a false alarm is merely reviewed, you buy recall with precision. mAP averages over all thresholds and so says nothing about which one to deploy.

questions.stem: What is hard negative mining?
choices: Collecting more positive examples
Focusing training on background regions the model wrongly scores as objects, rather than on the abundant easy background
Removing difficult images
Mining the dataset for duplicates
questions.explanation: Most background is trivially rejected and teaches nothing. Selecting the negatives the model currently gets wrong concentrates the gradient where learning remains. Focal loss achieves a similar effect continuously by down-weighting easy examples rather than selecting a subset.

questions.stem: Your detector performs well on the validation split but poorly on a new camera installed at a different angle and height. What is happening?
choices: The model is overfitting the training set
Domain shift: the new viewpoint, scale distribution and lighting differ from training, so learned appearance priors no longer hold
The NMS threshold is wrong
The model needs more classes
questions.explanation: Validation drawn from the same cameras cannot reveal sensitivity to a new one. The fix is data from the new conditions, augmentation spanning viewpoint and scale, or fine-tuning on the new site. This is why per-site evaluation matters in multi-camera deployments.

questions.stem: Why does a detector trained on 640x640 often degrade when run at 1280x1280 without retraining?
choices: Larger images always score worse
Object sizes in pixels double relative to the learned scale priors and anchor assignments, so the scale distribution no longer matches training
The model runs out of memory
NMS fails at higher resolution
questions.explanation: A detector learns what objects look like at particular pixel scales relative to its feature strides. Changing inference resolution shifts every object's apparent size. Multi-scale training makes a model robust to this; otherwise inference resolution should match training.

questions.stem: What is test-time augmentation in detection, and what does it cost?
choices: Augmenting the training set more heavily; it costs training time
Running inference on several transformed versions of the image and merging the detections; it improves accuracy at a multiple of the inference cost
Augmenting the labels; it costs annotation effort
Applying NMS twice; it costs nothing
questions.explanation: TTA typically runs flips and scales and fuses the results, recovering detections a single view misses. It multiplies latency by the number of views, so it suits offline batch processing and rarely suits a real-time pipeline.

questions.stem: How does DETR differ fundamentally from anchor-based detectors?
choices: It uses larger images
It treats detection as set prediction with a transformer and bipartite matching loss, removing anchors and NMS entirely
It detects only one class
It requires segmentation masks
questions.explanation: DETR predicts a fixed set of queries and uses Hungarian matching to assign each to at most one ground-truth object, so duplicates are penalised during training rather than removed afterwards. That eliminates both anchor tuning and NMS, at the cost of slow convergence in the original formulation.

questions.stem: What does mosaic augmentation do for detection training?
choices: Blends two images and their labels
Tiles four images into one, exposing the model to many scales and contexts per sample and placing objects at unusual positions
Converts images to a mosaic pattern
Splits one image into four training samples
questions.explanation: Mosaic composes four images spatially, so a single training sample contains varied scales, backgrounds and object placements including near the borders. Unlike Mixup it preserves coherent geometry, which is why it suits detection where Mixup does not.

questions.stem: Precision is high but recall is low on a new dataset. Which TWO are plausible causes?
choices: The confidence threshold is set too high for this data's score distribution
Anchor or scale priors do not match the object sizes present, so many objects are never assigned as positives during training
NMS IoU threshold is too high
The model has too many classes
questions.explanation: High precision with low recall means the model is confident when it fires but rarely fires. Either the threshold is filtering valid detections, or training never taught it these shapes because no prior matched them. A high NMS threshold keeps more boxes, so it would not reduce recall.

questions.stem: When mapping detections back to the original image after letterbox preprocessing, what must be undone?
choices: Only the resize
Both the scale factor and the padding offset, or every box will be systematically displaced
Only the padding
The colour conversion
questions.explanation: Letterboxing applies a uniform scale then pads to square. Reversing only the scale leaves every box shifted by the pad amount, producing boxes that look plausible but sit consistently off-target — a bug that is easy to miss on square images and obvious on very wide or tall ones.

questions.stem: Annotators disagree about whether partially occluded objects should be labelled. What is the consequence and the remedy?
choices: No consequence; the model averages it out
The model receives contradictory supervision for similar appearances, capping achievable performance; the remedy is an explicit annotation guideline and relabelling to it
The model will learn both behaviours correctly
Only recall is affected
questions.explanation: Inconsistent labelling means the same visual evidence is sometimes positive and sometimes negative, which is irreducible noise from the model's point of view. No architecture or training trick recovers it. Defining the rule — a visibility threshold, say — and enforcing it is the only fix.
